w: What's tested The goal of denture occlusion: keep a prosthesis that floats on soft tissue in the mouth, so balance means resisting tipping Support, stability and retention: what each resists, and why stability matters most How a denture stays in: the film of saliva and the border seal more than suction, good fit, and above all muscle control; what resists tipping Resorption patterns (maxilla up and in, mandible down and out), skeletal Class I, II, III and pseudo-Class III, setting teeth over the ridge Balanced vs non-balanced (neutrocentric) vs lingualized occlusion: contacts in centric and eccentric positions, anterior contact, teeth and articulator settings, who gets which, and the slides' table comparing them Centric occlusion, not MIP, in a denture; Hanau's Realeff: build and check the occlusion on an articulator; Thielemann's formula and which factors are fixed Denture teeth: porcelain, composite and acrylic; anatomic (30-33°), semi-anatomic (12-22°) and flat (0°) tooth forms; how the teeth are chosen 1 Support, stability and retention: what each resists, and stability matters most A professor's hint · 7 questions in the bank Know this Support: vertical force toward the tissues. Retention: dislodgement away from them. Stability: horizontal force. An unstable denture hurts and stops patients eating; retention problems bother them but don't hurt. Support Vertical force toward the tissues (closing and compressing the dentures) Some areas take it well: the buccal shelf and retromolar pad below, the palate above (the primary support areas); the ridges themselves aren't good at it Retention Vertical dislodgement, away from the tissues What patients focus on: peanut butter holds the dentures together as the jaw opens, the tongue lifts the lower denture. It bothers them, but it doesn't hurt Stability Horizontal force (sideways movement) The most important: a denture that slides sideways when they bite is extraordinarily painful, and they can't eat "Of all the things that we need to address, stability is the most important." It is the one thing a dental implant is fabulous at: even two implants address stability, and that is life-changing for a patient who couldn't eat. Retention from implants is a plus. Humans are among the worst for stability: we don't chew like a shark, straight up and down; we move the jaw side to side. Denture occlusion, the shapes of the teeth as they fit together, contributes to all three, especially stability. The three are related: tipping is a horizontal movement, and it can also dislodge the denture, which is retention. 2 The goal: keep the denture in the mouth; balance means resisting tipping A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this Denture occlusion keeps the prosthesis in the mouth; balance means resisting tipping. The mindset: denture occlusion is all about keeping the prosthesis in the mouth. The denture teeth are parts of an upper prosthesis and a lower prosthesis, each working as a single unit, so balance means resisting tipping, and stability is the property that matters most. Complete dentures start in January in the PCD course, with him. 3 Balanced vs non-balanced: contacts, anterior contact, teeth, articulator (his table) A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Non-balanced: flat teeth, flat plane, zero condylar guidance, so the patient's own guidance separates the teeth. Long maxillary lingual cusps on a flat or wide fossa; balanced or non-balanced; no anterior contact (in class: never; the slides: difficult, can be compensated). 2. Non-balanced occlusion. Contact in centric occlusion, but the denture is designed so it can't contact anywhere else: flat teeth, a flat occlusal plane, and an articulator set to something completely unlike the patient. The condylar guidance is set to zero; the patient never has zero, so whatever condylar guidance they have separates the dentures as they move. There is no anterior contact. Not contacting is another way to keep a denture from tipping. The slides also call it neutrocentric occlusion. In centric occlusion Posterior teeth contact Posterior teeth contact Maxillary lingual cusps contact the mandibular teeth In eccentric positions Contact on both sides (working and non-working) and in protrusion No contact in any eccentric position Balanced: contact in eccentric movements too (left-right balance); non-balanced: none Anterior contact Allowed in protrusion with anatomic teeth (the posteriors stay in contact); with semi-anatomic teeth only if the plane or curve compensates None No: difficult, though it can be compensated (in class: never, since it can't be kept from tipping front to back) Posterior teeth Anatomic (30-33°) or semi-anatomic Flat (0°) Semi-anatomic maxillary teeth with a long lingual cusp, against 0-12° mandibular teeth with a wide fossa Articulator Programmed to match the patient: semi-adjustable, facebow, protrusive record Condylar guidance set to 0° As for the scheme chosen Plane and compensating curve Used to keep the teeth together Flat: no compensating curve Flat when non-balanced; a little plane and curve to balance 4 Muscle control is the most important factor in keeping a denture in A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this Suction, adhesion and cohesion help, but they need good fit and aren't enough during function. Physical forces. The slides sort them. Contributing less: atmospheric pressure, vacuum, adhesion, cohesion and the seating force. Contributing more: the interposed fluid, the film of saliva between the base and the tissues (its flow, its viscosity and how thin the film is), and surface tension at the periphery. They depend on the patient's saliva (viscous or thin; it changes with age, and most denture patients are older) and on extension to the periphery: a good border seal keeps air from seeping under the denture and letting it drop or tip. All of them require good adaptation and a border seal. On a cone beam CT of a patient wearing a denture, dark spaces between the base and the tissues show misfit, and where there is misfit, suction and cohesion become almost impossible to capture. And most of them are undone in function, especially by hot liquids: even with good fit, they aren't strong enough to hold a denture while the patient chews. Muscle control. What really keeps a denture in is the musculature. Some patients develop neuromuscular control that keeps even the worst-fitting denture in place, and they eat fine; others can't manage the best denture you could make. "Muscle control is likely to be the most important factor to keep a denture in place." And remember: most of the time patients have their teeth apart, so adhesion, cohesion and muscle control are what hold the denture then. Two more points from the slides: undercuts in the ridge help only a little, and they can make the denture painful; and an ill-fitting denture makes resorption worse. 5 Resorption patterns, crossbite and pseudo-Class III A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this The maxilla resorbs up and in, the mandible down and out: a pseudo-Class III, and teeth set over the ridge, in crossbite if needed. Resorption follows patterns. The maxilla resorbs up and in, so its supporting arch gets smaller than the original arch; the mandible resorbs down and out, so at the level where the teeth are supposed to be, the edentulous mandible becomes larger than the dentate one. The slides give the direction for each region: Denture teeth are generally set near where the ridge is ("not rocket science"), so we often have to set them in crossbite, and that's fine: there's nothing wrong with a crossbite in a denture. The jaws also started out different sizes. A skeletal Class I (orthognathic) relationship has the jaws roughly matched in size and shape; in skeletal Class II (retrognathic) the mandible is smaller and set back; skeletal Class III (prognathic) is the opposite. These are related to Angle's molar classes. A patient who becomes a skeletal Class III because the mandible resorbs outward while the maxilla resorbs inward has a pseudo-Class III relationship. "What I want you to know today": the skeletal Class I, II and III relationships, and pseudo-Class III from resorption. All of this affects where the teeth go, which he will teach in January. 6 The maxillary anterior mold sets the rest, and it's chosen on esthetics A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank And the anterior mold is chosen more on esthetics than occlusion. Personality still shows up: every manufacturer's chart still has soft and bold molds (the temperamental theory, alive in 2026), and general shapes, square, tapering or ovoid (even combinations, "if you're the indecisive type"). The slides give six criteria for the posterior teeth: the color, in harmony with the anterior teeth; a buccolingual width less than the natural teeth; an occlusogingival length set by the interarch distance and in harmony with the length of the canine; a mesiodistal length that fills the space from the distal of the canine to the retromolar pad; the cuspal inclination; and the material. 7 Lingualized occlusion: easy to set, balanced or not, no anterior contact A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Which way to set it depends on what the patient brings. Non-balanced: a lot of ridge resorption, flabby tissues, poor oral awareness or dexterity, difficult jaw relations. Balanced: healthy, good ridges, firm mucosa, good awareness and good muscular dexterity. The slides list seven advantages: the centric contacts move half a tooth lingual, a more favorable lever; the force is centered over the ridge crest (slightly lingual in the molar area); there is only one contact point; minimal frictional contact; the maxillary buccal cusps are buccalized, leaving escape ways for food; working and balancing contacts are simpler, since only one cusp occludes; and it works with any ridge morphology, so with almost any patient, young to old. It is also easier to set. Disadvantage: with fewer teeth touching, wear shows sooner, and the patient may lose vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO). 8 Centric occlusion, not MIP, in a denture; CR is easy to find A professor's hint · 2 questions in the bank Know this In a denture: centric occlusion, with the joints seated (CR is easy to find). When the muscles of a denture patient contract, they seat the joints, so centric relation is pretty easy to find (most patients don't posture forward, though some skeletal Class IIs will). Contact of the denture teeth with the joints seated is centric occlusion: the joints seated and the denture teeth fully interdigitated, as best they're designed to. MIP is not a term used for dentures: maximum intercuspation is a neuromuscular response, and there is no neuromuscular response with a denture. 9 Build and check the occlusion on an articulator: Hanau's Realeff A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this Hanau's Realeff (resiliency and like effect): build and check a denture's occlusion on an articulator. Bilateral balance had been around a long time, but the person who made it easier was Rudolph Hanau, an engineer, not a dentist. He saw that you can't create the occlusion in the mouth, because the tissues keep moving: he named it the Realeff ("resiliency and like effect"). So the occlusion is built on an articulator. If you try to mark a denture occlusion in the mouth with articulating paper, the denture tips as it squeezes into the soft tissues, everything marks, and it gives you the wrong information; the denture course teaches the clinical remount instead. The slides add Hanau's own rules: his balanced occlusion used heavy contacts on the first molars to make up for the Realeff of the soft tissues and the joints, and the precise balance built on an articulator isn't present in the mouth, so it is refined through clinical remounts, never by adjusting the occlusion in the mouth. 10 Partial dentures: the more natural teeth remain, the more dentate the occlusion A professor's hint · 2 questions in the bank Know this Partial dentures: many teeth left, plan canine guidance or group function; few left, plan like a denture. Not everybody loses all their teeth. For a partial denture it's simple: the more teeth that have been lost, the more you think like a denture, an occlusion that keeps the prosthesis stable, with support, stability and retention. The more natural teeth remain, the more you think like the dentate patient: canine guidance or group function, and posterior disclusion, because the teeth are in charge, not the prosthesis. With implants, more factors come in: what the opposing arch is, how many implants were placed, and the reminder that every removable prosthesis has some motion, such as rotation. 11 All removable is movable: what resists tipping, the tongue, interarch space A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Structures have to be in the way to keep a denture from moving, and as they are lost, it gets harder. The slides list what resists tipping. Anatomy: the ridge height, ridge width and ridge shape, the depth of the palatal vault ("a big one for the maxillary denture") and the type of posterior palatal seal. Denture design: the fit of the intaglio surface, the side that rests on the tissues, and occluding contacts that don't move the denture. You will assess the anatomy in the denture course. Some tissues are more compressible than others, particularly toward the soft palate. Because heat-processed resin shrinks, a posterior palatal seal is added at the back to push into the soft tissues and overcome the shrinkage; milled dentures fit intimately enough that it isn't always needed. Two more factors you can't get around. The tongue hypertrophies after the teeth are lost ("nature abhors a vacuum"): it fills the space where the teeth used to be, mostly a problem for the lower denture. And a recent extraction patient, with plenty of bone, is not easier: they are often harder, because a denture needs room for its base and teeth, and limited interarch space makes it much more difficult. 12 The four schemes compared: the slides' summary table Core of the slides · 3 questions in the bank Esthetics +++ + + − Penetration of food + + + − Stability during function ++ + − − Simpler technique − − + ++ Less precise records − − + ++ Decreased lateral forces − − + ++ Ease of adjustment − + ++ +++ Class II and III jaw relations − − + + Stability with centralized forces − − + + 13 Non-balanced is neutrocentric: neutralize the inclines, centralize the forces Core of the slides · 3 questions in the bank So the non-balanced idea: allow contact only on closure into centric occlusion, separate in every eccentric movement, and keep the forces centralized, never lateral or horizontal. The neutralizing factors are the cusp angle, the plane of occlusion, the compensating curve and the anterior guidance, all made flat, and the articulator's condylar guidance is artificially set to zero. The slides give five tooth factors. Position: as far lingual as the tongue allows. Proportion: the buccolingual width narrowed by 40% to decrease the stress on the ridge. Pitch: parallel to the planes of the denture bases, with no compensating curve and no anterior guidance (the patient is told not to incise in protrusion). Form: cuspless. Number: the mandibular second molars may be removed to keep the occlusion flat ahead of the ascending ramus, which starts to rise there. That makes it very easy to set up. The old flat teeth weren't esthetic, but they functioned well even for patients without good ridge height. Today's flat teeth have functionally flat surfaces that don't look flat, and with most of the esthetics coming from the anterior teeth, they look fine. 14 Tooth forms (30-33°, 12-22°, 0°), their names, for and against, and choosing for the patient Core of the slides · 9 questions in the bank Cusp angle 30-33° (the handout: 30° or more): sulci, ridges, look like teeth Lower, about 12-22° depending on the mold (the 12° and 20° molds); lingualized maxillary teeth belong here 0° Scheme Balanced; can let the anterior teeth touch in protrusion Balanced or not; lower lateral forces; can't support anterior contact unless the plane or curve compensates Non-balanced For it Best esthetics; chewing efficiency (controversial); resist rotation of the base; guide jaw closure into centric; less force per unit area on the ridges; the incisal guidance can be balanced Easier stability; can still be set in balance Least lateral force, so stability is easiest; any jaw relation (Class I, II, III) and crossbite; simpler to adjust; poor neuromuscular control; fewer complications Against it Needs a protrusive record and a facebow on a semi-adjustable articulator; more skill (a technician sets one in 20 minutes, your first takes days); hard to refine; more horizontal force through the cusps, so more bone deformation; short-lived results as the denture settles and inexpensive teeth wear; difficult with abnormal jaw relations Not quite as esthetic Less esthetic (old ones "dog-ugly"); poor penetration of food, so more pressure on the ridges and more lateral chewing; difficult to balance; a psychological drawback for some patients. Clinically acceptable The slides cite a systematic review (Abduo, 2013, in the International Journal of Prosthodontics): anatomic teeth set in balanced or lingualized occlusion are preferable to flat teeth set non-balanced, mainly for patient acceptance. The literature is inconclusive but tends to favor cusps, and all the schemes are generally successful. 15 Hanau and Thielemann: the five determinants, which are fixed and which vary Core of the slides · 4 questions in the bank Know this Hanau's five determinants keep denture teeth together; for natural teeth, the same factors keep them apart. Hanau also gave us the relationships among the five determinants of occlusion (Hanau's quint). Thielemann's articulation formula (the one the Review lecture spells Thielmann) shows them as proportions: balance = (condylar guidance × anterior guidance) / (cusp angle × compensating curve × plane of occlusion). It first said incisal guidance; later, anterior guidance. Early on, cusp angle and cusp height were used interchangeably; today cusp angle is the term for dentures and cusp height for the natural dentition. The determinants were first used for their original purpose, keeping denture teeth together. For example, if you increase the plane of occlusion, then to keep the teeth together you flatten the compensating curve or use a flatter tooth. For the dentate patient we take the same principles and turn them around to keep the teeth apart: the same tool, used differently. 16 Denture tooth materials: porcelain, composite and cross-linked resin, acrylic Core of the slides · 6 questions in the bank Esthetics Very esthetic, often the most Good; layers improve translucency Fair; may stain Wear Minimal, so it maintains the vertical dimension Multi-cross-linked for wear resistance, but it still wears: in 5-7 years the teeth are worn to a reverse curve and chew inefficiently Less wear resistance Bond to the denture base None: held mechanically, with pins (anterior teeth) or diatorics, holes with undercuts (posterior teeth) Chemical bond Chemical bond to the acrylic base Handling May chip or fracture; denser and harder than crown and bridge porcelain, so difficult to set and adjust; clicks against each other Don't chip; softer sounds; easier to adjust and polish; expensive Low cost; easy to shape and adjust; can be ground to fit a small interarch distance Used for High-end dentures The most common: most good dentures today, the number one go-to Mainly temporary (interim) prostheses Also flagged in class Early dentures were made for esthetics; Bonwill made the first real attempt at denture occlusion. Every removable prosthesis moves on resilient tissue; it is designed to resist that motion. The balanced vs non-balanced (and lingualized) comparison: contacts, anterior contact, teeth, articulator. It is in the notes and Review. The mold chart engineers the mandibular anterior and the posterior teeth to match; the anterior mold is chosen on esthetics. Berry's ratio (central incisor about 1/16 of the bizygomatic width) and ala-to-ala: not valid, but they tend to look good. Anatomic teeth chew a bit better, but it isn't clinically significant; chewing is one factor of many. You can skip How to set the anterior (and posterior) teeth is the January denture course; know the principles here. The history (carved and sprung dentures, Washington's, porcelain, Bonwill, Gysi) won't be tested; keep the point: denture occlusion is about not tipping.
